definition: Programming computers to learn from experience (data) rather than from explicitly written rules.
details: Arthur Samuel defined the field in 1959 as giving computers “the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed,” demonstrated with a checkers program that improved by playing itself. Modern machine learning spans supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, and underlies almost every recent advance in AI.

explainer.lead: Machine learning means programming computers to learn from experience, i.e. data, rather than from explicitly written rules. Arthur Samuel defined it in 1959 and demonstrated it with a checkers program that improved by playing itself.

tiers.eli5: Instead of telling a computer every rule, you show it lots of examples and let it get better with practice, like a player improving by playing game after game.
tiers.practitioner: Practitioners span supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, and the approach underlies almost every recent advance in AI. A pitfall is forgetting that the learning depends on data and experience rather than explicit rules.
tiers.paperLevel: Arthur Samuel defined the field in 1959 as giving computers “the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed.” The field spans supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning.

explainer.example: Samuel's checkers program improved by playing itself, learning from experience instead of following hand-written rules.

citation.title: Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers
citation.venue: IBM Journal of Research and Development 3(3), 210–229
